raw_response:
I am still doing wheat-maize on all 10.1 mu. At my age, I do not want to gamble too much. I have seen enough years to know that if wheat misses water at the key stage, or maize goes hungry after wheat harvest, the yield drops fast and you cannot get it back later. The extension people say the rate more exactly, but on my land I still follow what has worked in past years and adjust a little by how the field looks. Since some people in my family work off-farm, I cannot make the management too complicated. I will keep the whole area in the usual wheat-maize rotation, use the local improved seed that is easy to buy, put most fertilizer in two splits, and use the well mainly at the important stages because pumping costs money. I would rather spend a bit on fertilizer and one or two timely irrigations than save that money and lose yield.

For wheat, I will sow in early to mid October after maize harvest, using rotary tillage and leveling because that is what fits my labor and machine access. I will put base fertilizer before sowing, then topdress once around jointing if the seedlings look normal; if the wheat looks weak or yellow, I will not cut that topdressing. I plan about three irrigations for wheat because in our place wheat depends on water more. For maize, the turnaround after wheat is tight, so I will not do deep tillage, just quick residue clearing and rotary tillage or direct planting with a hired machine if available. Maize I will fertilize in two times too, with one base application and one topdressing around the big flare stage. Usually maize can rely more on summer rain, so I plan one irrigation, and if rain is good that is enough. This way I keep costs in hand but still protect yield.
